title: AI's Power Problem: Who Pays for the Electricity?

headline: AI IS BRINGING BACK
*THREE MILE ISLAND.*
cta: AND YOU MIGHT BE PAYING FOR IT.

description:
In 1979, Three Mile Island became the worst nuclear accident in American history. Now a reactor at the same site is being brought back to life — to power Microsoft's data centers.

In this video: how much electricity AI really uses (the IEA's latest numbers), why AI chips are so power-hungry, the gigawatt campuses being built in Louisiana and Memphis, the nuclear deals from Microsoft and Google, and the grid auction that is pushing up power bills for 65 million Americans. At the end, three things to watch.

Information as of October 17, 2026. Sources: International Energy Agency, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, PJM Interconnection, U.S. Energy Information Administration, Constellation Energy, Kairos Power.

scenes.say: In March 1979, a reactor at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania partially melted down. It became the worst nuclear accident in American history.

The damaged reactor, Unit 2, never ran again. Its twin, Unit 1, kept running until 2019, when it shut down because it was losing money. Now Unit 1 is being brought back to life. Not for a city. For Microsoft.
Under a twenty year deal signed in 2024, Microsoft will buy the plant's power for its data centers. The restart is targeted for 2027.
Why would a software company need its own nuclear reactor? Because AI runs on electricity. A lot of it. And the bill is starting to land on people who have never typed a word into a chatbot.
This is the story of AI's power problem. How much it really uses, where that power comes from, and who ends up paying for it.
Chapter one. The number.
In 2025, data centers around the world used about 485 terawatt hours of electricity, according to the International Energy Agency.
By 2030, the agency expects that to roughly double, to around 950 terawatt hours. That's about as much electricity as the whole of Japan uses in a year today.
And AI is the fastest growing part. Last year, electricity use by all data centers rose 17 percent. For data centers built for AI, it jumped 50 percent.

In the United States, the shift is even sharper. Data centers used about 4.4 percent of the country's electricity in 2023. Researchers at Berkeley Lab, in a report for the Department of Energy, project that could reach between 6.7 and 12 percent by 2028.

visual.title: U.S. DATA CENTERS · SHARE OF ELECTRICITY
visual.source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory / U.S. DOE

scenes.chapter: Chapter 2: Why AI Is So Hungry
scenes.say: Chapter two. Why AI is so hungry.

A regular website runs on ordinary servers. AI runs on racks packed with specialized chips. Each one can draw around 700 watts or more, and thousands of them work together for weeks to train a single model.

A traditional server rack might draw around ten kilowatts. The newest AI racks can draw more than a hundred. That's roughly the average power use of a hundred American homes, coming out of a single cabinet.

And training is only the start. Every time someone asks a chatbot a question, makes an image, or lets an AI agent work through a task, more chips spin up. That's called inference, and as hundreds of millions of people use AI every day, it's a growing share of the load.

visual.title: WHERE THE POWER GOES
items: COOLING  ·  getting rid of the heat

scenes.say: All of that heat has to go somewhere. Cooling adds even more power on top of the computing itself, and, as we covered in our last video, a lot of water.
Put it together, and you get a new kind of customer. A single campus that wants as much power as a city, and wants it all day, every day.
Chapter three. The gigawatt campuses.
In rural Louisiana, Meta is building a campus called Hyperion. At full size, it's expected to draw as much as five gigawatts. For scale, the Three Mile Island reactor produces less than one.

To feed it, the local utility, Entergy, plans ten new gas fired power plants, about seven and a half gigawatts in all. Seven of them were announced in March 2026, and still need approval from state regulators.

visual.label: NEW GAS PLANTS PLANNED FOR HYPERION
visual.sub: ~7.5 GW in total · 7 still need state approval

scenes.say: In Memphis, Elon Musk's xAI powered its Colossus supercomputer with a fleet of gas turbines. Neighbors complained about air pollution, and in January 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency said generators like these are not exempt from permitting rules.

Others are betting on nuclear. Besides the Three Mile Island restart, Google has signed up for small modular reactors from a startup called Kairos Power. The first one broke ground in Tennessee in April 2026, and is scheduled to start delivering power in 2030.

events.text: Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart target

scenes.say: Notice the gap. The AI is being built now. Most of the new clean power comes later. In between, a lot of that demand is met with gas, and with the same grid everyone else depends on.
Chapter four. Who pays?

The largest grid operator in the United States, PJM, serves about 65 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C. Every year, it holds an auction to pay power plants to be ready years in advance.
For the year starting June 2024, that price was about 29 dollars per megawatt per day. For the year starting June 2025, it jumped to about 270. Then the next two auctions both hit a price cap.

In the auction held in December 2025, PJM came up about 6,600 megawatts short of what it needs for reliability. The first time that has ever happened across its whole system. By PJM's own forecast, about 5,100 of the 5,250 megawatts of new peak demand that year come from data centers.

visual.label: OF NEW PEAK DEMAND FROM DATA CENTERS (5,100 OF 5,250 MW)
visual.sub: Auction fell ~6,600 MW short of the reliability target

scenes.say: Those costs flow into retail bills. The U.S. Energy Information Administration expects households to pay around 18 cents per kilowatt hour on average in 2026, up nearly five percent. It also expects commercial buildings, which include data centers, to use more electricity than homes in 2027, for the first time on record.

visual.label: AVG. U.S. HOME ELECTRICITY PRICE PER kWh · 2026

scenes.say: Tech companies and utilities argue that data centers pay their own way, and that new demand helps fund grid upgrades. Consumer advocates say households are covering part of the cost. Regulators in several states are now writing rules to decide who pays what.

left.title: TECH & UTILITIES
left.text: Data centers pay their way and fund grid upgrades

right.title: CONSUMER ADVOCATES
right.text: Households are covering part of the cost

scenes.say: Chapter five. What to watch.

So, is AI going to break the grid? Not tomorrow. Even in 2030, data centers are expected to use only around three percent of the world's electricity. But the growth is packed into a few places, and it's arriving faster than new power plants can be built.

visual.label: DATA CENTERS' SHARE OF GLOBAL ELECTRICITY · 2030

scenes.say: Here are three things to watch. One. Whether the Three Mile Island reactor actually comes back on schedule in 2027. Two. PJM's next capacity auctions, and whether price limits stay in place. And three. Efficiency. Chips keep getting more efficient, but cheaper AI tends to mean more AI. Whether demand bends, or keeps climbing, is the big open question.

scenes.say: Forty seven years after Three Mile Island became a symbol of nuclear fear, it may become a symbol of something else. Just how badly AI needs power. If this was useful, subscribe to The Catalyst.
